summary: This standards-track document defines SIP response code 199, Early Dialog Terminated. A forking proxy or user agent server can send it to say that an early dialog has ended before the final response. Callers can then clean up state for that attempt.

eli5.summary: When a call rings several phones at once, some stop ringing early. Code 199 tells the caller that one of those ringing attempts is over.

questions: how to signal end of early dialog in sip
what does 199 early dialog terminated mean
why does a forking proxy send 199
subtitle: SIP response 199 lets forking proxies tell callers that one ringing attempt is over, before the final answer arrives.

tldr.problem: A forking proxy may hold back a non-2xx final response while it waits on other destinations, so the caller keeps resources reserved for an early dialog that has already ended.
tldr.mechanism: A forking proxy, or a UAS, sends a 199 Early Dialog Terminated provisional response naming the ended early dialog, but only to callers that signalled support with a 199 option-tag.
tldr.outcome: Callers can release resources or change media decisions sooner. It is only an optimization: since 199 may be lost, applications must work acceptably without it.

today: RFC 6228 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends RFC 3261 with the 199 response code and option-tag.

sections.title: The Problem with Silent Early Dialogs
sections.content:
In SIP, an early dialog is created when a non-100 provisional response is sent to an initial dialog-initiating request such as INVITE. It stays in early state until a final response is sent. A proxy that forwards a request to several destinations is forking it, as defined in RFC 3261.

When a forking proxy gets a 2xx final response it forwards it and normally sends CANCEL to the other destinations that have not answered. A non-2xx final response is different: the proxy may store it and wait for other destinations, then pick the best final response later.

Meanwhile the caller and other upstream entities are not told that the early dialog has ended, so they keep resources reserved. Those resources could have been used for something else, such as accepting later early dialogs they would otherwise reject. RFC 6228 defines response code 199 Early Dialog Terminated to close this gap.
sections.eli5: Imagine you called three friends at once and one hung up, but nobody told you. You keep holding a spot for them. A 199 says, "that one is done."

sections.title: An Optimization, Not a Guarantee
sections.content:
The 199 response is described as an optimization of how quickly recipients learn about terminated early dialogs, and the gain is limited. A UAS normally does not send it reliably and a proxy cannot send it reliably, so some or all 199 responses may be lost. If so, recipients behave as if 199 were never used.

Application designers who use 199 MUST make sure the user experience is acceptable if every 199 is lost. A UAC might use a received 199 to release resources, or to switch to playing media from a different early dialog.
sections.eli5: 199 is a helpful heads-up note that might get lost in the mail. Everything must still work if it never shows up.

sections.title: Caller and Callee Behavior
sections.content:
UAC. A UAC willing to receive 199 responses MUST put a 199 option-tag in the Supported header field of the initial request. It SHOULD NOT put it in Require or Proxy-Require, since that would often cause needless session failures. It is also RECOMMENDED that the UAC not put 100rel in Require while supporting 199, because proxies are not allowed to generate 199 when provisional responses must be reliable.

After accepting a 199, the UAC MUST NOT send media for that early dialog and, if it can tell, MUST NOT process media received for it. There is no need to send BYE for that early dialog. Other early dialogs are unaffected. An unreliable 199 on a dialog the UAC does not know yet SHALL be discarded.

UAS. If the request's Supported header carries 199, the UAS SHOULD NOT send a 199 before a non-2xx final response, except where configured to (for example, because forking proxies lack support) or where an environment requires it. If the option-tag is absent, a 199 MUST NOT be sent. A 199 from a UAS MUST have a To tag identifying the early dialog and a Reason header field with the response code explaining why it ended. It SHOULD be sent unreliably unless 100rel is in Require.
sections.eli5: The caller raises a hand saying, "I can understand 199 messages." Only then may anyone send one. When one arrives, the caller stops using that one attempt.

sections.title: Forking Proxy Behavior
sections.content:
When a forking proxy receives a non-2xx final response that ends one or more early dialogs, it MUST send a 199 upstream for each ended early dialog that meets all of these conditions:

  • the proxy does not intend to forward the final response immediately;
  • the UAC signalled 199 support in Supported;
  • the UAC did not require reliable provisional responses with 100rel;
  • the proxy has not already received and forwarded a 199 for that early dialog;
  • the proxy has not already sent a final response for any of the early dialogs.

The proxy tracks early dialogs by the top Via branch value of the responses that created them. If the same value appears for several early dialogs, more forking happened downstream, and a non-2xx final response for one also ends the others sharing that value. A proxy MAY wait before sending a 199, for example if it expects a 2xx on another dialog shortly.

The generated 199 MUST contain a To tag for the ended dialog and a Reason header field with the SIP response code that triggered it. It MUST NOT carry a 199 option-tag in Supported, Require or Proxy-Require, and SHOULD NOT contain Contact or Record-Route. A proxy receiving a 199 handles it like any non-100 provisional response and MAY release resources for that dialog.
sections.eli5: A switchboard operator who hears that one phone gave up passes that news to the caller, but only if the caller asked for such news and the operator has not already given the final answer.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and SDP
sections.content:
Not every entity understands 199, so the sender MUST be ready to see further requests and responses on that dialog. A UA that receives such a request MUST act as if it had sent a non-2xx final response to the INVITE, as in RFC 3261. A UAC that has received a 199 MUST NOT send more requests on that dialog, except to acknowledge reliable responses. A proxy MUST still forward requests per RFC 3261, even if it knows the early dialog ended. A 199 does not replace a final response.

For SDP, a 199 SHOULD NOT contain an offer or answer unless RFC 3264 requires it. If an INVITE had no offer and the 199 would be the first reliable response, the UAS SHOULD send it unreliably, or send it reliably with an SDP offer that has no m= lines.
sections.eli5: Some people do not know the 199 code, so everyone must still behave sensibly if the other side acts as though nothing was said.

sections.title: Message Flow Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three flows. In the first, proxy P1 forks an INVITE to UAS_2, UAS_3 and UAS_4, which all send 18x responses. UAS_2 and UAS_3 reject with 4xx, and P1 immediately sends a 199 for each, then forwards the 200 from UAS_4.

In the second, UAS_4 answers 200 OK first. P1 forwards it and sends no 199 for the other two dialogs, since it has received no final response on them and they could still produce a 200.

In the third, P1 forks to UAS_2 and to a second proxy P2, which forks to UAS_3 and UAS_4. P2 does not support 199 and forwards a single 4xx. P1 associates both early dialogs with it and sends two 199 responses.
sections.eli5: The examples show a switchboard telling the caller about each phone that gave up, and staying quiet when a phone has already been answered.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: General SIP response issues are in RFC 3261. Because 199 ends a specific early dialog, it may be attractive for attacks that terminate chosen early dialogs; other early dialogs are not affected. If a man-in-the-middle sends a UAC a 199, it can take a while for the UAS to discover that the UAC and any stateful intermediaries have dropped the dialog. SIP security mechanisms such as hop-by-hop TLS can minimize or eliminate the risk.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky could shout "that one hung up!" to make you drop a real call attempt. Locking the line with encryption helps.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers a SIP response code and an option-tag under the procedures of RFC 3261.

  • Response code 199, default reason phrase Early Dialog Terminated, defined in RFC 6228.
  • Option-tag 199, which indicates support for the 199 provisional response. In Supported it says the UAC supports 199. In Require or Proxy-Require it means the UAS or proxies MUST support 199, but it does not require them to actually send one.
sections.eli5: The new code number and its matching "I understand it" flag were added to the official lists so everyone uses the same ones.
